title: Is D.C. Really An Education Reform Success Story?
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler examines a Mathematica study that the Washington Post cited as proof that Washington D.C.'s market-based reforms worked. She grants the study some credit for showing gains in early-grade math and reading beyond what demographic change would explain, but notes that the gains disappear by eighth grade and that NAEP data is a problematic tool for judging a specific reform. Her central argument is that the study ignores what is taught and how. Reading tests reward general knowledge and vocabulary, and reform-era pressure to raise reading scores drove schools toward drilling abstract comprehension skills instead of building knowledge, so students from less-educated families fall further behind each year. She adds her own classroom observations on the costs of the IMPACT teacher-evaluation system, high turnover, disruptive charter closures and a weak district-built literacy curriculum. She closes by proposing the experiments researchers should run, comparing knowledge-building and systematic decoding instruction against the standard approach.
points: The Mathematica study found early-grade gains but no extra improvement by eighth grade and no high school conclusions, which falls well short of proof that the reforms worked.
Wexler's core claim is that reform focused on test scores reinforced a skills-first view of reading comprehension at the expense of building knowledge, especially in elementary grades.
Students from highly educated families absorb academic knowledge at home, so schools that do not build it leave other students farther behind each year.
The study overlooks reform costs she observed, including stress and turnover under the IMPACT teacher evaluation system and disruptive charter closures.
Her proposed remedy is experimental, comparing knowledge-building curricula and systematic decoding instruction against standard approaches, and talking to teachers.
quotes: But even if you accept Mathematica’s methodology, the study falls far short of proof that the reforms “worked.” It did conclude that scores rose in fourth- and eighth-grade math beyond what would be accounted for by demographic change.
In reading, the results were even less impressive: scores rose at fourth grade but not at eighth. Given the importance of reading ability to learning in general, that finding is sobering.

Students from more highly educated families typically absorb that knowledge at home, giving them an advantage on standardized tests. If kids from less-educated families aren’t acquiring that kind of knowledge at school, they fall farther behind every year.

The D.C. Public School system’s teacher evaluation framework, called IMPACT, may have helped push out a few “ineffective” teachers, but it was also unfair to many others—especially at the high school level, where educators were faced with the impossible task of getting woefully unprepared students ready to graduate within four short years. Teachers have told me that the resulting stress has been a big factor in D.C.’s extremely high teacher turnover rate.

To be fair, some DCPS officials have tried to discourage a focus on such skills. But rather than adopting one of the knowledge-building elementary literacy curricula created by curriculum experts in recent years, DCPS created its own version—and from what I’ve seen, it falls far short of those created by experts.

With only 30% of fourth-graders scoring at the proficient level or above on the most recent NAEP, one commentator has declared that D.C. is facing “a reading crisis.” And that crisis is clearly continuing to affect different student groups differently: 79% of white fourth-graders scored proficient or above, but only 19% of Black students and 27% of Hispanic students did.

How about comparing one group of students that gets a knowledge-building curriculum beginning in kindergarten to another group that gets the standard approach, as has been done in some other districts? Or comparing one group that gets systematic decoding instruction against another that doesn’t? And maybe try talking to some D.C. teachers and observing some classrooms.
